speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my hard and indeed melancholy duty to inform the house officially of the passing of one of our parliamentary colleagues who was, I think, a friend of us all; Jack Garland, the Minister of National Revenue. He was a man who was young in years but a veteran in service to his community and his country, having been a member of this house now for more than 14 years.
Jack Garland was the last person I saw on Friday night as I was walking down the corridor to go home, and the last word I had with him was to receive from him an assurance that he thought he had found a way of helping some householders who were in difficulty over their mortgages in a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation housing project. This was typical of him, because he was always trying to help people.
I think the best evidence of the quality of a man is his reputation among those with whom he has lived, and any visitor to North Bay would have learned at once how Jack Garland met that test, how he was regarded in his own community with warmth, admiration and affection by everyone. He had earned and won their deep respect, and that feeling of admiration and respect was,
I think, shared by every member on all sides of this house, because we were all his friends.
As a member of the house he was courteous and painstaking in the discharge of his duties. As a ministerial colleague he was quietly competent, firm but conciliatory, with the good judgment and the common sense that had made him successful in business. Mr. Speaker, he was a big man in every sense of the word and he was a good man in every sense of the word. He was a gentle man and he was a gentleman, generous and kind, and we shall miss him sorely.
I send, Mr. Speaker, our heartfelt sympathy to his mother and father who survive him, and above all to his wife, who shared his life so fully and devotedly and who is now bearing such a heavy burden of grief. We send her our deep and heartfelt sympathy as well as our prayers at this sad time for her.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems strange that two of the younger members of the house should be the first to be taken in the present parliament.
Jack Garland was indeed a friend to everyone. He enjoyed the respect of all members regardless of their party affiliations. He gave the same attention to the requests of those who disagreed with him as he did to those who politically agreed with him. As the Prime Minister has stated, he was here for 14 years, and during that time he built for himself a reputation as a kind, gentlemanly person, a man whom all of us were proud to call a friend. I could repeat the eulogy of the Prime Minister in toto. I simply say that, in the words he used he epitomized the views of Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
To the widow and to his parents goes the sympathy of this house in their bereavement. Parliament was a better place because of his presence. Of no one can more be said.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext:
All of us were shocked and saddened by the news of the death of Hon. J. R. Garland, Minister of National Revenue. It is a sad occasion when any man is cut off in the prime of life, but it is especially so when that man is of the calibre of Jack Garland. He was one of the most popular ministers in the government. His friendliness and sincerity impressed all of us. We admired him for the efficient and conscientious manner in which he discharged the responsibilities of his office.
I am sure many hon. members have had the experience of raising some matter in the house pertaining to the Department of National Revenue or to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, only to receive a phone call in a few hours and hear a warm, friendly voice saying "This is Jack Garland. I am calling you to tell you what we are doing about the matter you raised in the house." Any irritation one might have felt melted away in the presence of this kindly man who was so clearly doing a job and doing it well.
The House of Commons will be the poorer for his passing. We mourn him as one we could ill afford to lose, and one whose contribution to the public life of Canada merits our admiration and commendation. The members of the New Democratic party extend to his wife and relatives, to his constituents

The Late J. R. Garland and to his colleagues in the government our deepest sympathy at the great loss which they have sustained. We too feel we have lost a good friend and a worthy colleague.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext:
We join with the Prime Minister, with the Leader of the Opposition and with the leader of the New Democratic party in expressing our sorrow and our regret at the passing of John Garland.
Certainly all that has been said is true and characteristic of this man. I would say personally that it has been worth being here just to have known him. He was a big man, a big man in every sense of the word, too; entitled to be called a gentleman, a man whose heart reached out to the welfare and need of others.
Two things that happened in the last few days will mark my memory of him. One was a conversation just outside the doors of the chamber where we stopped to speak about a problem, and I am sure he had many similar problems brought to his attention. After he had explained his position we talked a little about his health, and he assured me that he was physically well and enjoying the heavy responsibilities of the difficult position of Minister of National Revenue. The other was to open my mail this morning and find a letter from him, which must have been signed on Friday afternoon before his passing, and to be thus reminded again of how faithful and careful he was in discharging his responsibilities.
Personally and on behalf of the members of the Social Credit party I extend our sympathy to his widow, to his parents and to the Prime Minister and each member of his party in the untimely passing of one of the most distinguished members of the house. All of us consider it something to be proud of to have been counted as one of his friends and to have been associated with him.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sudden and untimely death of the Hon. John Richard Garland took everybody by surprise. We all got to know him in this house and, for my part, I had known him since 1949.
Mr. Garland was still relatively young and his passing came as quite a shock to us all, both in this house and outside. In the federal cabinet he headed a department which is not too popular in Canada and yet he had gained for himself the reputation of being a man of integrity and a hard worker. As the leaders of the other groups in this house have just said, I think all hon. members always enjoyed meeting him and talking with him, because

he was obliging and dealt squarely with problems we brought to him.
To his father, his mother, his wife, his whole family and his electors in Nipissing, we extend our most sincere sympathy. We truly regret that he will no longer be with us.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. R. GARLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Jack Garland was out of the Ottawa valley. As is our traditional tragedy, he left the valley to seek a livelihood. The people of the north took him to their hearts, and their gain was our great loss. On behalf of myself and my people I offer to Mrs. Garland and his loved ones our condolences. Jack Garland was of a rare and singular breed of men. He was by nature, by inclination and in practice a gentleman. We, his friends of the valley and all of us here, shall miss him.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
On February 25 last, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam, I promised to make a statement to the house regarding the future of the Colonel Belcher hospital in Calgary as soon as the government was in a position to be specific on the action it intended to take in this regard. The interest shown both inside and outside the house concerning the future of the hospitals operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs is such that I think a general statement at this time could do much to clear misunderstandings and remove misgivings.
No one is more conscious than the government of the magnitude of the debt we owe to those thousands of Canadians who were prepared to sacrifice their lives to preserve the integrity and way of life of Canadians. Many thousands of these men never came home. For those there is nothing of a tangible nature we can do except perpetuate their memory and make provision for their widows and children. But for those who did return, many of them mentally or physically crippled for life, there is a lot that can be done. Indeed, a lot has been done. The body of legislation collectively known as the veterans charter, designed to rehabilitate returning servicemen back into civilian life, has been remarkably successful.
Not the least of these tangible expressions of gratitude are the treatment services of various kinds that have been made available to disabled veterans. Veterans hospitals have

Statement on Veterans Hospitals come to mean different things to different people. They were originally designed to assist in the over-all project of rehabilitation back into civilian life, and to provide a continuing source of treatment for service incurred disabilities. With the passage of years, and as space became available, the facilities have come to be used more and more by veterans without service connected disabilities, particularly by those who qualified for treatment on the basis of indigency. This was a praiseworthy activity and one which would gladly be continued, were it not for the fact that the nature of the patient load on our hospitals today is beginning to threaten our ability to provide the kind of treatment which the war disabled veteran is entitled to receive.
I think we might profit by casting a quick glance at what happened to veterans hospitals between the end of world war I in 1918 and the beginning of world war II in 1939. As many hon. members will remember, our veterans hospitals progressively deteriorated until, during the last few years before the outbreak of world war II, they had earned a deservedly unenviable reputation.
This was due to a number of different causes. Undoubtedly the most important of these was that as the years went by the nature of the patient load in these institutions shifted from one which was predominantly active to one made up, in the main, of veterans suffering from chronic illnesses for which little could constructively be done, or who were too aged and feeble to look after themselves. In short, the complex of our hospitals had gradually changed from a series of well equipped institutions staffed by energetic and competent groups of men and women to a series of rest homes with obsolescent facilities and to which it became virtually impossible to attract high calibre medical specialists and nursing staff.
We must profit by that lesson and not repeat that mistake. The standard of treatment provided by the department in its hospitals since the end of world war II has been extremely high. It is my earnest desire, as it is that of my colleagues and, I am sure, of all hon. members that this should continue to be so. However, the likelihood of our being able to maintain this high standard as the nature of the patient load changes is becoming more and more problematical. Veterans hospitals are now used mainly for the accommodation of older veterans-and many of us are reaching that stage-with long term, chronic ailments which generally speaking are not a result of their military service.
As a consequence of the changing nature of this patient population, recruitment problems are becoming alarmingly acute, particu-
[Mr. Teillet.l
larly in the nursing classes. We are coming dangerously close to the unhappy situation which prevailed in veterans hospitals just prior to world war II. Indeed, had it not been for the sense of dedication of the really first class group of men and women who staff our institutions, we probably would have witnessed by now the beginning of a disintegration in the quality of the medical service provided to our veterans. This must not be allow to happen because, in the final analysis, the one thing we must ensure at all costs is that those veterans who were disabled as a result of service to this country should be provided at all times with the best medical care this country can muster.
At this time the best way-indeed, the only way-to maintain this kind of excellence is to make the treatment of veterans an integral part of a larger, more active, more on-going operation; in other words, to incorporate the treatment of veterans into treatment programs devised for members of the general community. If this is not done the professional stimulus that is essential to the fostering and maintenance of first class medical service will be lacking, with the obvious result that the veteran will be the loser.
Despite many suggestions to the contrary, the federal government cannot and should not become involved in the operation of general community hospitals. Consequently the only practical solution to the very real problem we face is to enter into agreements with suitable agencies to take over the operational control of veterans hospitals. These would then become general community hospitals, in which the department could purchase the service it must provide.
At this point I would like to make it unequivocally and emphatically clear that no such agreements will be entered into by the government unless certain sine qua non conditions are met. These conditions, three in number, are as follows: First, accommodation for the treatment of service connected disabilities among veterans must be immediately available at all times, and treatment must be provided in accordance with standards prescribed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Second, community institutions of acceptable standards must be available to look after the work load created by other classes of veterans, which means that such veterans will be able to obtain treatment in their own communities, near their own friends and families. Finally, satisfactory arrangements must be made for the continued employment of professional and other staffs now serving in our institutions.

From what I have said up to this point it will be clear where the best interests of disabled veterans lie. It so happens that by serving the best interest of the veterans in this fashion the department will, at the same time, be able to lend valuable assistance in relieving the shortage of active hospital beds which is becoming apparent in some of the metropolitan areas in Canada. It would be folly, to say the least, not to make our hospital facilities available to the non-veteran population where the need is so great, when this can be done while not only maintaining but also improving the quality of treatment services provided to our veterans.
The question of timing is of great importance. Our hospitals are still first class institutions; their staffs are still of first class quality. We are in a better position now than we will be a few years from now to ensure the kind of conditions we think essential in any transfer. Moreover, many communities need active treatment facilities now, as is borne out by the fact that discussions which have recently taken place have all been initiated by authorities other than federal. I am sure informed observers of the situation will agree, keeping in mind the best interests of veterans as well as the hospital needs of the community at large, that the most propitious time to make such arrangements is sooner rather than later, provided the three essential conditions referred to earlier can be met.
It is therefore the view of this government that the operational control of veterans hospitals should be transferred to non-federal agencies at times, in places, and under conditions which will best protect the standards of care to which veterans are entitled.
In conclusion I would like to refer to a number of allegations which have recently been made to the effect that the government had changed its policy on treatment services for veterans. Nothing, of course, could be further from the truth. The government's policy can be stated quite simply and quite clearly. That policy has been, is today and shall continue to be that the government is determined to spare no effort to provide the best possible medical service for our veterans within the framework of statutes enacted by this parliament. If, in order to achieve that end, the methods employed to provide such medical services must be changed, then change there shall be. But whatever happens, our ex-servicemen and the Canadian people generally can rest assured that we shall employ every legitimate means at our disposal to carry out that policy to its fullest extent.
I feel confident that no member of this house would have it any other way. I feel equally confident that the Royal Canadian
Statement on Veterans Hospitals Legion and other responsible veterans organizations would not have it any other way. Certainly this government would not have it any other way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure this announcement will be received with dismay by veterans and their relatives across this country. I think this is a complete reversal of the policy followed for so many years by successive governments in the care of the veterans of this country, whether they are veterans of the first world war, the second world war or the Korean war.
I am rather shocked at some of the phraseology used in his document. It is the first time it has ever been brought to my attention that the veterans hospitals "during the last few years before the outbreak of world war II had earned a deservedly unenviable reputation". This is a shocking condemnation of veterans hospitals, which have had a high reputation for over 40 years; and it is a condemnation of the activity of former Liberal governments to express the position in terms of that nature.
But the main factor that emerges from this statement by the minister is that the policy in existence for so many years is now going to be changed. Changed at whose wish, or by whose whim? This is not the wish of the veterans in this country.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
The stand that our party took when we first read the summary in the Glassco commission report that there might be some change in the veterans hospitals was "Hands off the veterans hospitals". We continue to take that stand. I am surprised that the Minister of Veterans Affairs should consider that veterans other than those who have disabilities resulting from warfare are not also possibly suffering from war experiences and war exposure. Not every man who served overseas was wounded visibly. My experience with veterans of two world wars shows that there are a great many men who have been suffering all these years from the strain of active service. They may not show that by the loss of a limb or some physical disability, but the strain is there.
I am very much disappointed that the government should at this stage, with this haste, declare that it is going to change the situation with regard to the veterans hospitals across Canada. This is a matter which should have been considered very thoroughly by

Statement on Veterans Hospitals the standing committee on veterans affairs of this house. It is before that body that the veterans organizations should come and present their case. The standing committee on veterans affairs should visit our veterans hospitals in Canada and see the situation for themselves. A hasty program like this is an insult to the veterans of Canada.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think this is a political question.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
I am sure it has been under study for some time by the medical director of D.V.A., even before the present government came into office. Therefore it should be looked at dispassionately and in the light of the best interests of the veterans whom these hospitals were designed to serve.
I think one must face the fact that there are some problems which the government has with reference to veterans hospitals. Increasingly they are becoming less and less active treatment centres and more and more centres for treating chronic illness; but in my opinion this does not justify turning all of them over to other authorities, and for two reasons. One is that there are a great many veterans who need continuing care and who ought to be cared for in institutions along with their former comrades. Second, I think there are a great many veterans of the last world war and of Korea who will require increasing hospital care in the years ahead, and there ought to be institutions to which they can go.
The danger is that if all the veterans hospitals are incorporated into general community hospitals there will not be beds available for these veterans. Perhaps the answer is to turn some of the veterans hospitals into hospitals for chronically ill veterans present and future who will require custodial care, and make arrangements for other hospitals to be incorporated into active treatment centres for the general community.
The one thing I would urge upon the minister-and I make this plea to the Prime Minister-is not to allow a snap decision to be made on this matter, because it affects a body of men and women to whom this country owes a great debt. I hope this whole matter will be thoroughly studied by the standing committee on veterans affairs so that no policy will be pursued which we would later regret. I trust that no action will be taken that would result in a situation where veterans would find that when they required hospital care, it was not available to them because these hospitals had been turned over to communities who had filled them immediately and not left sufficient beds to take care of the veterans.

As I say, I hope the government will send this matter to the veterans affairs committee, where not only members of the house can study the matter but where the veterans organizations, the D.V.A. itself and the medical director can make their views known to the members of that committee.

Mr. Speaker, we realize that this is not the opportune time to debate the announcement which has just been made. As far as the reaction of many veterans across the country is concerned, I think it would be found in these words, that "The thing I most fear has come upon me". Many veterans have expressed their views, I am sure, to all members of the house relative to the proposals which are now before us, and have voiced serious concern over the fact that consideration was being given to turning the veterans hospitals over to civilian agencies.
In presenting his statement this afternoon the minister outlined three considerations, and I think they are very worth while. The main one is that in the event of such a change, veterans would be assured of immediate hospitalization and medical care of the highest quality. I think this is one of the main considerations which must enter into this picture.
As far as the entire principle is concerned, I believe this proposal should be referred to the veterans affairs committee before any definite action is taken in this regard, and before government policy is crystallized. It would be interesting-

subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS RESPECTING MEAT PACKING INDUSTRY
RECOMMENDATIONS RESPECTING MEAT PACKING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Is the government considering implementation of the recommendation made in the report of the restrictive trade practices commission on the packing of meat, Wilsil Limited and Calgary Packers Limited in 1961 that "the possibility of seeking a court order under section 31(2) of the present Combines Investigation Act be fully explored for the purposes of dissolving the mergers of Calgary Packers Limited and Wilsil Limited with Canada Packers" and further "in the event that it is determined that such a remedy cannot be sought the commission would recommend that the possibility of seeking a court order under section 31(2) be fully explored for the purpose of prohibiting Canada Packers from making any further acquisitions which would lessen competition in the meat packing industry"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS RESPECTING MEAT PACKING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
In 1956, the director under the Combines Investigation Act commenced his inquiry into the acquisition by Canada Packers Limited of Wilsil Limited and Calgary Packers Limited. The matter was, in due course, referred by the director to the restrictive trade practices commission which made its report to the minister on August 3, 1961, which was subsequently made public as required by the Combines Investigation Act.
The commission recommended that-
-the possibility of seeking a court order under section 31(2) of the present Combines Investigation
Act be fully explored for the purpose of dissolving the mergers of Calgary Packers Limited and Wilsil Limited with Canada Packers. In the event that it is determined that such a remedy cannot be sought the commission would recommend that the possibility of seeking a court order under section 31(2) be fully explored for the purpose of prohibiting Canada Packers from making any further acquisitions which would lessen competition in the meat packing industry.
Since publication of the commission's report and recommendations, very careful study has been given to the question of the legal proceedings, if any, that should be taken. The matter was referred to leading counsel with instructions to proceed with prosecution or other criminal proceedings unless he should come to the conclusion that the evidence is insufficient. Full consultation took place between counsel and the departmental officials and the opinion was ultimately received that legal proceedings would be unlikely to succeed. This view was confirmed by an opinion obtained from second leading counsel.
In the circumstances I have felt bound to arrive at the conclusion that it would be unwarranted to subject the company to criminal proceedings when on the basis of expert opinion it appears unlikely that such proceedings could succeed.
I should add that my decision is largely influenced by jurisprudence on the merger provisions of the Combines Investigation Act that has developed since the merger took place and the inquiry was commenced.

speechtext: Was a four year study made of year round navigation in the gulf of St. Lawrence and along the St. Lawrence river to Montreal by the glacio-logical section of the geographical branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and, if so, what was the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: STUDY OF WINTER NAVIGATION, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: No study has been made by the geographical branch on the feasibility of year round navigation in the gulf of St. Lawrence and along the St. Lawrence river to Montreal. The glaciology section of the branch has conducted airborne studies of the distribution of ice in these waterways, strictly from the point of view of statistical analysis of the ice distribution itself and the relative importance of the various climatic parameters involved. These studies were initiated in 1956 and are being carried out during the current year. A series of research reports (geographical papers Nos. 11, 12, 14, 16, 19, 23, 25, 32 and 36) have been published, giving the complex results of these studies. I would emphasize, however, that no attempt has been made to relate the problems of ice distribution with that of the feasibility of year round navigation, as this is outside the area of our responsibility. Copies of the research papers can be supplied on demand.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that was seen, yesterday, on the French television network when the Governor General was delivering his speech; we could see then two flags, the flag of the United Nations and the union jack of England.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING EQUALIZATION OF OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING EQUALIZATION OF OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: I am grateful to the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. The teachers federation brought this matter to my attention before the last provincial conference, and at that time I agreed to inquire of the provinces whether it was a matter which they thought should be discussed or a matter which fell within their jurisdiction, that is the equalization of educational opportunity. I did that, and there was no reaction on the part of the provinces to put the subject on the agenda of the forthcoming conference. It is my view that while the federal government has an interest and its own responsibilities in certain phases of the subject, a discussion of this kind should be initiated by the provinces since they have jurisdiction in this field. If the provinces or a province would initiate such a discussion, and put it on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference, we would be glad to participate in that discussion.

Mr. Chairman, on Friday last while the Minister of Finance was out of the house and his colleague was "subbing" for him, I asked a number of questions and I asked for an undertaking by the minister-

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in order to save the time of the committee- to have replies to those questions either mailed to me or tabled later in the house. I wonder whether the minister could give me an undertaking that the questions I asked on Friday will be answered either by letter or by tabling the answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must apologize to the hon. member. I have not the answers yet. However, I will look into the questions and write the hon. member at the earliest possible opportunity. I hope he will forgive me if that is not until tomorrow.

Certainly, Mr. Chairman. Some of the questions I asked concern, of course, other ministers and I would be quite happy to have replies from his now seatmate, for instance, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because a good many of the questions concern his department. As long as I have the undertaking, I am quite happy.

Mr. Chairman, I read in the press various articles on a situation now prevailing in the province of Quebec, to the effect that the provincial authorities do not seem to co-operate with the federal Department of Citizenship and Immigration, as in other provinces, in order to encourage immigrants to settle in the province of Quebec to the greatest possible extent.
I would like to ask the minister if he intends or has already taken steps to have a special office set up in the province of Quebec-as is the case in Ontario, for instance- which would co-operate with the minister's department, so that Quebec would get its share of immigrants and help them obtain the same privileges as in the other provinces?

Mr. Chairman, as my predecessor explained before, it is this government's policy to seek the fullest co-operation of the provincial departments to establish an immigration policy. We shall always be happy to see all the provinces answer the wish expressed by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. minister a supplementary question. Has the government of the province of Quebec expressed the desire of having an immigration office, as I asked before now?

I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is up to the provincial authorities to indicate their policy. As far as our own policy is concerned, it has already been made known, and I think that it is not appropriate for a federal minister to suggest the policy to be followed to a provincial government.

Mr. Chairman, I have another supplementary question.
The minister mentioned last week, that more provinces had expressed the wish to receive French speaking immigrants from Algeria. Could he tell the house whether certain provinces, among which Quebec, actually made a request to that end?
Mr. Chairman, I explained my position with regard to this matter last week.

Mr. Chairman, I have several questions in connection with the proposed Indian claims commission that I should like to ask now and perhaps they could be dealt with together. I should like to ask how many replies in general have now been received from the Indian bands in connection with comments on the draft legislation which was sent out, and also how long the minister intends to wait for replies. In other words, to what date have replies been requested. Third, has there been a follow-up letter sent to those Indian bands which have not yet commented on the draft legislation?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot say exactly how many replies we have received from the Indian groups to whom a letter had been sent asking their views on the setting up of the claims commission. They are still being received in the department.
As far as the second question is concerned, we asked in our letter that replies be forwarded before April 30, 1964.
In regard to the last problem raised by the hon. member, I wish to say that we will always be pleased to receive comments from interested persons before the bill is resubmitted to the house for consideration.

I wonder whether I might ask just one more question. Can the minister tell us whether there will be any indication to the house as to the nature of the replies which he is receiving from the bands? I refer in particular to questions such as the two year limitation period on claims which may be made, which may thereby wipe out existing claims which have been there for 200 years. Has there been any comment on this particular subject, or are the comments which the minister has received ranging widely across the bill?

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of such consultations is to permit the government to take note of claims and comments presented by the various Indian groups

before taking a final decision on this bill which the house has already considered to some extent. Such comments are made directly to the minister, and I have already indicated their nature to the house.
The recommendations and comments are considered by the minister and he will personally bring them to the attention of the cabinet in order that the bill, as amended, may be submitted to the house. Those consultations are, therefore, intended to inform the government and will not be made public.

Mr. Chairman, on Friday I asked the minister for reassurance on one or two points and before the item passes I wonder if he could give me that reassurance. That is all I want him to do. I would just repeat my points briefly. Will he reassure the house that he is prepared to take up with the officials of his department the possibility of making an administrative decision whereby the rates of financial assistance to the Indian people of this country shall be no less than the rates being offered non-Indians in identical circumstances in the same community? I am not asking him for his decision; I am asking him to reassure the house that he will take a reading on this possibility, because I am satisfied that all that is required is an administrative decision.
I am also satisfied that no member of this committee would oppose or chastise the minister if in his next estimates he asked for those funds which would allow him to see to it that the Canadian Indian people will not be treated as second class citizens when qualifying and applying for financial assistance. That is the first reassurance I am requesting.
From the minister's answer to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka I take it that the time limit his department will set before introducing the legislation in respect of the Indian claims commission will be April 30. He has indicated to the Indian people that he wishes to have their views by then and that at that point the department will not wait any longer before bringing this legislation before the house.
The third point on which I ask for a reassurance is that his department will look into the possibility of setting up a contingency fund to provide for the costs of legal expenses incurred by those Indian people who require to go to court in certain areas. There are many areas in Canada in which we are not sure whether, for example, the provisions of the Migratory Birds Convention Act prevail or the treaty signed with the Indian people, and until such time as the Indian claims commission is a reality and has a
16. 1964	955
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration chance to examine the claims of the Indian people, which will be a matter of a few years, there will from time to time be those cases where the Indian people will want to appeal from decisions of lower courts. Therefore I want the minister to assure the committee and to assure the Indian people of Canada that the cost of legal services to present their case adequately will be provided to them. I hope the minister can do that before this item passes.

Mr. Chairman, as regards the first point raised by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) concerning Indian welfare measures, I agree with him that the problem is not a simple one, although I am in complete agreement with him when he says that the Indians and other Canadian citizens, must be placed on an equal footing in regard to welfare benefits. It is precisely for that purpose that a federal-provincial conference will be held in May where the federal government will try to seek the co-operation of provincial governments so that in future, the Indians may profit from some adjustments in regard to the benefits given the citizens of other provinces in the field of social welfare.
As far as the second point raised by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories on community developments is concerned, we are quite pleased to say that this program is the very basis of our policy for the Indians. We followed with a great deal of interest the plans worked out in Manitoba and Saskatchewan on community developments.
We will be quite pleased, during our coming negotiations with the provinces, to find out how we could speed up those community development programs.
I might say that in the department, we are now reviewing all our Indian services in the light of the new policy which is being worked out.
As for the third point, that is payment by the federal government for legal services provided Indian groups who have to bring claims before the courts, this poses a more difficult problem. It is a very serious problem which was brought before the department on various occasions by the Indians.
We have a team working on that particular problem, in view of the new legislation to be brought before the house concerning Indian claims.
There are many facets to that problem. I am not yet in a position to announce the departmental policy in this respect, but I can
956	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration assure the hon. member that we do our best to help those Indian groups as far as this matter is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to call to the minister's attention a court case which took place in my constituency last week concerning an alleged offence by Indians in the way of contravention of the provincial game act. They had been convicted in the magistrate's court. Two of them had chosen to serve jail sentences in preference to paying fines. Others had been fined. Last week, Judge Swencisky of the Supreme Court of Canada-
The county court.

The county court; pardon me. Judge Swencisky reversed the decision of the magistrate's court and ordered the refund of the fines to those who had paid fines. He also expressed the view that if, as was, I think, indicated in court, the crown in British Columbia were to proceed to appeal this case to a higher court, then in his opinion the Indian affairs branch should foot the bill for the defence by these Indian citizens against that appeal.
I wonder if the minister could tell us whether his department has discussed this possibility-whether the matter has yet come to his attention-and whether anything has been done, too, with regard to providing some compensation for the men who had chosen jail sentences, instead of paying fines, so as to be consistent with the judge's order that fines should be returned to those who had paid them.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have details here concerning the specific case raised by the hon. member. However, I can say that in cases where Indians were faced with actions taken in courts by provincial authorities, we follow these cases very carefully and we await final judgment, either in the lower courts or in the appeal courts.
But if reference is made to the more general problem of our position in relation to the rights the Indians may have with respect to fish and game, we will be very happy, when the commission of Indian claims is set up, to introduce a general policy on Indian affairs with respect to the established rights of Indians in the field of fish and game.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, I would like to repeat the question I directed last week to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who was


advising me of his government's policy towards immigration, following an announcement by an employee of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to the effect that an amount of $300,000 or more would be spent besides the amount granted annually, in order to attract more British immigrants to Canada.
An advertisement appeared in the press about five or six weeks ago, I believe, to the effect that the government would spend an additional $200,000 or $300,000 in England in the country to attract British immigrants to Canada.
I know that the government at the present time maintains seven offices in England to attract English immigrants to this country. There are also five offices in Germany and one in each of the other countries in which we are interested.
I would really like to know, from the minister, how the government intends to proceed in future to encourage nationals of other countries to come to Canada, so that there may be not only one group.
In France, where the population is almost identical to that of England, I find that we have only one office to attract immigrants and attend to the necessary publicity to induce French immigrants to come to Canada.
There is also Italy, where people readily expatriate themselves. In that country, there is a population of over 50 million people, and yet, we have only one immigration office there.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that if the government intends to instil a little more life into its immigration policy and to make a somewhat more appropriate selection of prospective immigrants to Canada, it should also consider other countries where there are possibilities of attracting interesting individuals who would become an asset for our country.
England is not the only source where we can find good citizens for Canada. I have no intention of discriminating in any way against British citizens who are coming to settle in Canada; I am convinced that they are excellent citizens.
On the other hand, we should consider opportunities of attracting equally good citizens from France, Belgium and Italy.
I think that the government should make available greater facilities to help the immigration offices in those countries do a better job.
In recent articles published in the press, it was said that the employees of our immigration offices in Europe, on the continent, were travelling about from place to place and had no real interest in administrating Canada's immigration policy, as they had

been sent there as a good riddance. Even here, in Canada, they would not have been taught a very definite policy nor given the necessary funds to administer the immigration program that had been indicated to them. On the whole, those people in the various Canadian immigration offices in Europe are more or less frustrated in their jobs.
I would like the minister to tell us what his intentions are regarding the policy he wants to promote for attracting to Canada other people than citizens of the British Isles.

Mr. Chairman, the basic policy of the present government in the field of immigration is surely to increase publicity in countries likely to send us qualified immigrants. And this also entails an increase in the number of offices and of personnel.
Traditionally, this immigration has been directed towards certain European countries most likely to provide us with the type of immigrants required for the industrial development of Canada.
We intend to maintain this immigration policy in European countries, to increase the number of offices in France and in addition, to keep on looking into the possibilities of immigration from new or older countries which have not yet provided a great number of immigrants.
In other words, we are now revising our whole immigration policy precisely to be better able to determine the possibilities, in men, which the various countries of the world offer us in order to attain our objectives.
I thank the hon. member for pointing out to the department the need to increase its publicity and its activities in some European countries.

Permit me to speak in the same vein as the hon. member who was addressing the committee a few moments ago. I was pleased to hear him suggest that we should broaden the opportunities available to nationals of other countries who wish to enter Canada. I was pleased to hear him support this open door policy. Of course I do not believe any Canadian government could take effective steps to increase the flow of immigrants from iron curtain countries in central and eastern Europe. I have in mind Ukrainians, Lithuanians, Estonians, Latvians and others such as came here before the world war, established themselves here and are now making a splendid contribution.
I am all in favour of setting up more offices in France, Italy, and other countries from which larger numbers of immigrants might be expected to enter this country. I say this because we have wide open spaces;
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration we have lots of room and if we do not encourage these people to come, those in the congested areas of Asia will be looking across the Pacific and wondering why we keep them out.
I referred to a press report that the government of Manitoba had indicated a willingness to welcome a certain number of Algerian refugees. I hope that is correct. Manitoba is one of the most cosmopolitan provinces in our dominion. People of all races live there as Canadians with no squabbling. In fact, they are not even trying to set up a separate state of Manitoba or anything like that. We would welcome the Algerians, but there is some concern in Manitoba and other parts of the west over one matter and I should like the minister to give me an answer.
Does the admitting of Algerian refugees to Canada entail any expense on the part of the government? I know these people are unwelcome in Algeria, which has become an independent state after the revolution which lasted for five or six years. I can understand the situation of these people. Are they coming in as sponsored immigrants, are they coming in on their own or are they going to be supported as refugees in the same way that we supported the Hungarian refugees from Budapest after the 1956 rebellion had failed? I think this matter should be clarified for the people of western Canada, because they want to know the answer.

speechtext: First of all, may I say I agree with what my hon. friend said about the various peoples who now comprise the Canadian nation. I happen to have the privilege of representing a riding where the people come from all sorts of different origins. As the hon. member was speaking and as the hon. member for Lake St. John was speaking I was thinking particularly of the Italians, Ukrainians, Lithuanians and those from other iron curtain countries, as well as the French and the British, and may I add another minority group, the Scots.
By all means, the Scots.
What do you mean, minority?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the particular point about the Algerians, my understanding is that the French government itself is assisting financially the emigration to this country of the people to whom the hon. member refers.
Are they assisting them only to the extent of coming to this country or will they be assisting them to become established?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I want to address a very few remarks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and in doing so to support what was said by the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for the Northwest Territories with regard to the Indian claims commission. I recognize that the minister has not had too long at his task. The department is a very complex one and I wish him every success in his efforts to deal with the problems that come before him.
I want to suggest that he and his officials take a most careful look at what the terms of reference of this commission will be. Some of the litigation which has been referred to, some of the actions, some of the trials, stem from matters which should have been in the hands of an Indian claims commission at this time. I was a member of the joint committee on Indian affairs and we considered many of these contentions over a period of years. Many of the matters which were brought to our attention by the Indians have now been ventilated in court.
I refer in particular to the case which was brought to the attention of the minister by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. If the minister will recall, on March 6 I brought this specific case to his attention and asked him if he and his department would consider engaging counsel to represent these Indians, because a very important principle was involved. That principle was whether or not the royal proclamation of 1763 applied. If it did apply, then the entire issue involving a lot of the crown lands in British Columbia would be brought before the courts for adjudication at one time or another and some very serious questions might arise as to the status of these lands. This is one of the issues which was brought to the attention of the Indian affairs committee.
There is also a recent case from the supreme court of Manitoba decided by the Supreme Court of Canada as to the right of Indians to hunt and trap on certain unoccupied crown lands. It is interesting to note that in that case many of the attorneys general filed briefs. The attorney general of Quebec filed a brief in which he took the position that the Indians in Quebec were subject to all of the provincial game laws with respect to hunting, fishing and trapping. The brief filed by the attorney general of the province of Quebec flies right in the face of the Quebec Boundaries Act of 1912.
Then there are some decisions by a very distinguished jurist in the Northwest Territories, Mr. Justice Sissons, formerly a member of the house, and other decisions in Ontario as well. In other words, there are a number of issues involving Indians. There is

the question of the treaties signed in western Canada which, as I read them, quite plainly purport to give the Indians the right to continue to fish, hunt and trap in the provinces of western Canada. As far as Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned, the natural resources were transferred by the federal government to the provincial governments, and the provincial governments by their game laws which they say apply have in effect curtailed what seemed to be rights guaranteed to the Indians by these treaties.
These are all matters which I would suggest to the minister should be encompassed within the four corners of any terms of reference in connection with the Indian claims commission. It is not just that these Indians should be compelled to go to the expense of engaging counsel, of having to appear before the trial judge, then the appeal division of the province and finally the Supreme Court of Canada in order to test the validity of the stand they have taken for many generations, namely that these are rights to which they are entitled.
If in framing the terms of reference of the Indian claims commission the minister and his officials narrow and restrict them I believe they will be doing an injustice to the Indians and to the people of Canada who want to see the Indians get a reasonable break, justice and equity. I suggest to the minister that he should give the most careful consideration to the terms of reference so that all matters now remaining to be decided can be brought before this commission and settled once and for all.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the opportunity of the discussion of the supplementary estimates to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration one or two questions. I appreciate, as do other members, that the minister has only recently taken on the responsibility of this important portfolio and I should like to take the opportunity to wish him all good luck in the carrying out of that responsibility.
I have two matters which I think are of very great importance in the administration of the Immigration Act and I should like to ask him about them. First, can the minister say whether he and his department are considering amendments to the Immigration Act, and regulations to eliminate the remaining traces of discrimination on racial grounds from the act? I think this is something that is long overdue, and I hope this matter is being given consideration.
As for the second point I wish to draw to the attention of the minister, I believe there is need for the amendment of the act so as to provide that hearings on deportation cases

and cases of application for admission to Canada should be the genuine hearings which I think parliament contemplated in the Immigration Act. They should be hearings which have the true nature of proper hearings in accordance with the principles of the bill of rights and the fundamental principles of justice. That means that those who are being dealt with should have some idea of the reasons for deportation and the reasons for their exclusion.
I know there are difficulties about this matter but at the moment, in my experience, many of these proceedings are of a highly farcical nature. I will enlarge on this when the estimates of the minister come before the committee. I hope he is looking into this matter now and that we can anticipate action.
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for having called the attention of the house to those problems which will soon be looked into seriously by the government.

I have a very brief question for the minister, which I think will come under the heading of field inspectional services abroad. Are all the employees of these offices abroad Canadian citizens? If the answer is no, then do the powers of those employees, who are citizens of the country in which the office exists, extend to the determination of whether or not applicants will be rejected? I am thinking particularly of a situation that exists in Hong Kong at the moment. I understand that some of the employees in the offices there are not Canadian citizens, but they are allowed to rule on some of these applications. Is this right or wrong?

Mr. Chairman, I do not have the details at this time concerning the parts played respectively by Canadian citizens and citizens of other countries in our offices abroad. However, I do know that often, in those offices, local staff is hired to help with the work. But, if I am not mistaken, I think the people responsible for those offices are always Canadian public servants and that local persons to whom are assigned less important duties, are only hired to assist the Canadian personnel in the performance of their duties.

I have a matter to take up with the minister at this time. I realize that time is short, but I bring it up on this occasion because I believe an opportunity presents itself at this time to solve one of the 20220-61i
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration urgent problems confronting the Indian people in northern Manitoba as well as those in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. For a long time now, in co-operation with my colleagues who represent constituencies which encompass Indian reservations, I have been endeavouring to bring electric power to some of these Indian reservations. We have had some measure of success, but nothing which would merit the thought of laying down on the job at this time.
When we first approached the department, it was understandable that their attitude was they were not really responsible for providing such services to these communities, and they should not be charged with the responsibility for setting up power lines, distributing power, setting rates and collecting moneys. This seemed a reasonable attitude, although we felt the Indian affairs branch did have an obligation along this line. However, the province of Manitoba has managed to overcome these difficulties, and I hope other provinces can do so as well. We have an agency to look after the power lines, set rates, collect moneys and distribute the power, provided surplus power is available. When nursing stations and hospitals were being built on reservations, we asked that provision be made in connection with those establishments for the generation of sufficient surplus power to accommodate the needs of the adjacent communities. I must say that we have not had too much co-operation in this regard. I hope that in future we will get more co-operation.
The reason I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister today is that I believe an opportunity is being provided to make electric power available to many areas. Mention has been made recently of the drastic change which has been made in the operation of the mid-Canada radar line, with the dropping of the towers at the doppler sites. It is probably not generally known, however, that at each of these towers there were three diesel power generating units located. In northern Manitoba alone there are some 17 of these doppler sites that have been abandoned and the towers have been dropped. However, at each of these sites there are three diesel power generating units, which would mean that there are something over 50 of these diesel units sitting out in the bush of northern Manitoba.
I do not believe these units have been declared surplus as yet, but eventually they will be and they will go to Crown Assets Corporation. There will be a lot of people across Canada scrambling for these units. I believe it is the duty of the Indian affairs

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration branch at this time, in co-operation with the Department of National Defence, to alert Crown Assets Corporation that the Indian affairs branch has a definite interest in these units. The units from these 17 different sites in northern Manitoba would produce enough power for all the Indian reservations in northern Manitoba at the present time. There are one or two of these reservations which have power. Many of these areas that are without power now will be without power for many years unless this action is taken.
I think if co-operation can be arranged between the Department of National Defence and the Indian affairs branch so that these generators could be turned over to Indian affairs at a nominal sum, the problem would be solved. If the Indian affairs branch feels it cannot take the responsibility for bringing these units on Indian reservations, I think I can assure them that the Manitoba hydro would be very pleased to meet with federal authorities to do this job, provided the generators would be turned over to them. I know that money will be necessary and possibly it could be provided by the individual Indian reservations. Some of these people have band funds, but some of them probably are not in a position to go ahead with this project at the present time. I have thought, too, that the centennial commission is going to allot moneys to the provinces for certain projects and I can think of no better project for the Indian people of northern Manitoba than the bringing of power to these reservations. I hope, then, in conjunction with the minister it will be possible to obtain grants and, in this way, provide a very worth while and lasting service to these people. I hope that action can be taken by the minister before these units are declared surplus and are disposed of to the public. One or two communities on the Hudson bay line are also interested, but there are sufficient emits for all.

There is just one point I want to draw to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I do so at this time rather than wait for the main estimates because the Prime Minister has indicated the minister is making a trip to Hong Kong. I ask him to see if there is not something that can be done in order to permit the children of some of the families who are already in Canada to join them. These children are in Hong Kong now as refugees and they are not allowed to enter Canada because they cannot prove their identity. I have drawn some specific cases to the minister's attention. These children do not have papers, birth certificates or any other positive proof of identity.
When the minister takes this trip to Hong Kong I would like him to inquire whether

something could be done to relax this rigid regulation a little, so that children of families already in Canada can be brought in. Perhaps even on compassionate grounds some of these children could be allowed in, if they are healthy, and if there are families in Canada which would guarantee their support, even though the children cannot produce positive proof of belonging to these families.

I congratulate the minister on his appointment and wish him success in his important duties. In order for him to have success I should like to ask him to help solve two problems which I have run across in my riding, and which are not conducive towards increasing the country's population with desirable new citizens.
In my opinion both this and the former administration were at fault in these cases. The first arose in September-October 1962, and the second came to my attention just the other day. In the first case a successful businessman, a Greek who has been a Canadian citizen for the past ten years, and who is living in Napanee, applied to have his niece admitted from Australia. She was born in Greece and went to Australia under the pretence of getting married, but when she got there she found that the man who had been picked out to marry her was old enough to be her grandfather and she refused the proposal of matrimony.
Her uncle in Napanee made certain guarantees to the department in order that she might be permitted to come to Canada. I know these people; they are neighbours of mine and live across the street from me. I gave them a good recommendation as guarantors of this girl, but to no avail, as we were turned down by a deputy minister.
It seems to me that ministers are not properly employing their executive prerogatives in cases like this, when we can obtain new citizens of good repute, and I feel the minister should be able to bend the rule a bit.

You mean, use common
sense.

Yes, a proper use of common sense, especially in the case of female immigrants who are biologically conducive to increasing the population of this great country of opportunities.
The second case concerns a Spanish girl. Some Spanish constituents of mine applied for permission to bring a niece from British Guiana, but only the other day they got an answer from a civil servant, not from the minister or the deputy minister but from someone further down the echelon in the department, refusing permission.

I shall be in touch with the minister on this matter and I can guarantee him that she has no criminal record. She is in good health and she is not a communist. We know that the government of British Guiana is somewhat along those lines, but this girl is not a communist. She has high school education and is capable of doing many classes of work. She is bilingual. She speaks Spanish and English, and that is another form of bilingualism, but I must say I do not know whether she speaks Gaelic.
I submit that this is another desirable type of citizen which we are letting slip through our fingers. It has always been a problem to get more people of desirable stamp into the country, and I suggest that we get together and right some of these departmental wrongs. I say to the minister, let him use the common sense that goes with his prerogatives in the execution of his very important duties.

I wish to add my words in support of those of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Because of the ethnic nature of my constituency I handle a great many immigration cases, the majority of which are Chinese. I ask the minister to use a little bit of what I would call common sense, with blood in his veins, not ice water, in arriving at ministerial decisions on these matters.
I have particularly in mind the case of a Chinese Canadian who has been living in my constituency for many years, and who has been trying since 1951 to bring over one of his sons from Hong Kong. The trouble he is encountering is one I run up against all the time, that the authorities do not believe it is his son. How, in the name of heaven, if he comes from a village in mainland China, are you going to prove this? It is impossible.
Since 1951, when he first made application, this man has been sending 100 Hong Kong dollars every month for the maintenance of his son, and I cannot believe that a man will send 100 Hong Kong dollars a month from 1951 to 1964 to maintain his son, if the boy in question is not his son. I know the minister is in this office just a little while, but I would ask him to keep his mind open. These people present a picture of the relative they want admitted, and who in the name of God can tell by a picture whether or not it is the son of the father? It is hard enough to tell with whites, but it is almost impossible with Chinese.
I see it is five o'clock, and since there is another question I wish to raise I shall do so when we resume.
