subtopic: INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of including mental hospitals and t.b. sanatoria in the federal hospital insurance program (Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act) so that the provinces will have available sufficient funds to provide for adequate treatment of the mentally ill, those people suffering from t.b., and the care and training of mentally retarded children.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has been estimated that half of the hospital beds in Canada are now being used for the care of people who are mentally and emotionally ill. If we add those who are in t.b. sanatoria and those who are mentally deficient the percentage is even higher. In 1960 the house debated and adopted a resolution moved by the present Speaker of the house, the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton), which called for the co-operation of the federal government with the provinces and specialists in the field of mental health in "a survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment". That survey was conducted on behalf of the Canadian Mental Health Association by Dr. Tyhurst, a professor of psychiatry at the University of British Columbia, the survey having been issued under the title "More for the mind". This

Expansion of Hospital Care Program, is a report which ought to be studied by every hon. member of this house in view of the tremendous cost of mental illness to this country.
Dr. Tyhurst recommended that the patient suffering from mental illness should receive the same excellence of medical and ancillary health services as quickly, easily and as efficiently as the patient suffering from physical illness. Although this was his recommendation, Mr. Speaker, he pointed out that today mental illness is all too often considered a crime to be punished, a sin to be expiated or a disgrace to be hushed up. We have not yet calculated the cost to this country of mental illness, but according to the figures recently supplied for 1961, the last year for which we have any record, the cost of hospital care alone for mentally ill patients was over $150 million per year. This does not take into consideration the tremendous cost of medical services, loss of income through inability to work, cost of suffering to families and to the people who are mentally ill. We are spending, as I say, $150 million per year on people who are hospitalized because of mental illness. Yet, Mr. Speaker, if you compare the cost of a day's care in a general hospital with that in a mental hospital, you can see how little we have really considered the needs of the mentally ill. In 1961 the cost of keeping a patient in a general hospital was over $23 a day; the cost of keeping a patient in a mental hospital was just $5.90 a day. And we gave to those patients precisely what they paid for; we gave them no more than $5.90 worth, a day, in care.
Experience in the last 15 or 20 years has demonstrated conclusively that mentally ill patients can be treated successfully, can be brought back to well being and enabled to get back to work and to live with their families; but this has been done, not in the provincial mental hospitals as we have known them but mostly in the psychiatric wings of the general hospitals, which have been growing at a very substantial rate. It has been done in these hospitals because we have provided the services for them. We have provided a fairly adequate number of psychiatrists and social workers, psychologists and trained psychiatric nurses, which we have never provided and are still not providing in the provincial mental hospitals. Unfortunately these needs are precisely what we are not providing for the vast majority of the mentally and emotionally ill patients who have had, because of a lack of facilities and lack of money, to enter the provincial mental hospitals.
In the province from which I come-the province of Manitoba, which is no worse and probably no better than other provinces- according to a brief presented to the royal

commission on health services by the Manitoba psychiatric association there were only 27 qualified psychiatrists in the province. This is not more than two years ago. These people had to look after 3,000 patients in the provincial mental hospitals, 1,100 patients in the schools for mentally defective, as well as those people ill at home or in psychiatric wings of general hospitals. The province had established positions for 26 qualified psychiatrists in the provincial service, but there were only eight actually working in the provincial mental hospitals. Of these eight, four were doing administrative work almost exclusively. In one of the hospitals which I know very well, which has 1,200 patients, two years ago there were only three qualified psychiatrists on the staff and only two qualified social workers. So that even if a patient was lucky enough to get better and could have left the hospital, very often there was nobody who could make the arrangement for him to go into the outside world, help him to find a place in which to live, to find a job and help him learn to live again in the outside world. This is not an isolated case; the same is true in every province and in almost every provincial mental hospital in Canada. I am not being critical of the staffs of mental hospitals. I think they are doing a tremendous job within the realm of their ability, having regard to the tremendous staff shortages under which they are working.
The needs in the field of mental health for more active treatment of mentally ill patients can be met only by a very substantial increase in the number of trained personnel to treat mentally ill people. The present provincial mental hospitals, with their hundreds, or almost thousands of patients, which were established in the small towns or rural areas many years ago must be replaced by small community hospitals of 100 to 200 beds located in the larger cities or towns in Canada, to which trained personnel can be attracted.
The Canadian psychiatric association, in its brief to the royal commission, emphasized this point very well. I quote from the statement which can be found on page 5 of their brief:
In 1957 the federal government announced its program of hospital insurance and specifically excluded mental hospital patients from the benefits of this form of financial support. The consequences of this exclusion include a disparity in standard of care between the psychiatric divisions of general hospitals and mental hospitals, with secondary effects in terms of lessened recruitment of medical and ancillary personnel, and diminished incentives for program development and research inquiries within the mental hospital. The exclusion represents a continuance of segregation attitudes towards the mentally ill on the part of political and health authorities.

They recommend that federal-provincial hospital insurance programs be amended to include mental hospitals. To meet the needs of the mentally ill we need to double the number of doctors specializing in psychiatry by 1970. Training grants for students in this field need to be sharply increased. To accomplish this, the number of teachers in the field must be increased very sharply. Educational grants for this, according to the Canadian psychiatric association, will have to be tripled by 1970. A similar increase is needed for the training of additional clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers, occupational therapists and psychiatric nurses. No single step could contribute more to the improvement of the treatment of mentally and emotionally ill patients than the inclusion of these patients and the hospitals in which they are treated in the benefits of the federal hospital insurance legislation.
Dr. Tyhurst's report for the Canadian Mental Health Association put it as follows:
Exclusion of mental hospitals from the benefits of the federal hospital Insurance legislation accentuates the differences between the general and mental hospitals. It has the added psychological effect of contributing to the sense of difference which the patient feels and to the general stigma associated with mental hospitals.
The Canadian psychiatric association's brief to the royal commission on health services recommended as follows:
That federal-provincial hospital insurance programs be amended to include mental hospitals.
If this were done, Mr. Speaker, and if the provinces could be-and I think they could- persuaded to maintain at least their present levels of spending in this field of mental health, we would indeed see the dawn of a new day for those people unfortunate enough to be struck by mental illness; a day in which they could have the same hope for quick and permanent recovery from their illness as people who are physically ill. That day would be a great one for them and for the Canadian people as a whole.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on the hon. member's notice of motion. I would first of all like to congratulate him for bringing this matter forward, and I would like to say that I agree with this proposal in principle. At the present time-as the hon. member has stated-mental disease and tuberculosis are two of the three things that are excluded from the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Both these diseases have been little understood by the general public, both tending to be dealt with as though the patient had leprosy. This raises the question of why these two diseases were originally excluded from the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic
Expansion of Hospital Care Program Services Act. I cannot really answer this question, except to say that I would think it is probably because both these diseases are of a chronic nature and at the time of the passing of the act, in 1957-58, they meant long periods of hospitalization with usually little hope of cure.
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to read from a statement made by the previous minister of national health and welfare, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), to the special committee on estimates on Tuesday, March 8, 1960. He was dealing with this very problem and listed six reasons for the federal government's not wanting to take part in bringing tuberculosis and mental illnesses under this act. The first reason given was as follows:
The government has been faced with implementing a very complex and far reaching project, a task that would have been made more difficult by any substantial change in its existing terms.
Mr. Speaker, this act came into force in 1958. This is now 1964, and surely the administration of the act has now become simplified to the point where it would not create a great problem to include two more diseases and two more groups of hospitals in the benefits provided by this act. The second reason given by the previous minister was as follows:
The inclusion of tuberculosis and mental hospitals in the insurance program would have little financial effect on patients themselves. In 1D57, only 9.4 per cent of operating costs of mental hospitals and 2.4 per cent of operating costs of tuberculosis sanatoria came from self-paying patients. The bulk was met out of provincial revenues.
This raises an interesting question of who actually pays for the patients, for instance in a tuberculosis sanatorium. I was quite surprised to receive a request from a constituent regarding an immigrant he wanted to bring to Canada. This is where the question arose. The immigrant came from Italy, where tuberculosis is much more prevalent than it is in Canada today. The person who wanted to come to Canada had a questionable X-ray and it was considered possible, although not very likely, that he would require treatment, in this case in the Weston sanatorium. The guarantor, who was asked to guarantee the care of the immigrant, had to assure the Department of Citizenship and Immigration that not only would the immigrant be admitted to the hospital within three days of coming to Canada, but he had to post a $1,000 bond and guarantee to pay any balance of the hospital bill that might be incurred. Despite this fact, the minister at that time pointed out that in many cases the treatment of tuberculosis in individual cases can be very expensive, is part of our program for health

Expansion of Hospital Care Program and as a rule was met by the provincial government, together with other hospitalization. The third reason put forward by the then minister was as follows:
Almost one half of the funds available under the tuberculosis control and mental health grants are being used currently for the support of services in sanatoria and mental institutions.
As far as federal assistance is concerned, in 1962 the mental health grant was increased to almost $9 million. On the other hand, the tuberculosis control grant was decreased in 1962 to approximately $3,500,000. I think this points up very vividly to all hon. members that the problems of tuberculosis, thanks to the newer drugs such as streptomycin and the drug commonly known as P.A.S., are coming under better control; hospital and sanatoria beds are being closed and converted to other uses. However, the care of mental disease is becoming a greater problem.
The next point made by the minister, No. 4, was:
More than $36 million has been approved under the hospital construction grant for some 25,600 new beds in these institutions.
We have been talking a great deal in the house lately about anomalies. It seems to me it is another anomaly that federal assistance under the hospital construction grant program should be the same whether it is in respect of active treatment, treatment of chronic cases, mental cases or tubercular cases. Why the full grant should be given in these instances, while being withheld under the hospital insurance act, I do not know.
Point No. 5 made by the minister was:
Both tuberculosis and mental hospitals are in a state of transition. The t.b. death rate has declined dramatically and, as a result of new methods of treatment, a portion of sanatoria beds is being left empty. Psychiatric units in general hospitals are becoming more and more prominent and, to illustrate this trend, in one recent year, 1958, almost one third of all mental patient first admissions and readmissions were to these units.
I should like to add some figures to the figures already quoted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). In 1962 returns were reported from 83 mental hospitals showing a total of 67,739 beds. In the same year, 49 tuberculosis hospitals reported a total of 10,673 beds. Also in that year, 1,027 general hospitals reported a total of 103,551 beds. If these figures are studied it becomes clear there is a great discrepancy between the number of beds being used for psychiatric care and those listed as being in mental hospitals. This arises because a great many mental patients are now being cared for in general hospitals. This brings out a further anomaly. While patients who receive treatment for tuberculosis and mental diseases, in tuberculosis or mental hospitals, are excluded

from benefit under the health insurance act, those same patients, if they were admitted to a general hospital, would be qualified for benefits under the act.
The sixth point which the minister brought up was as follows:
Tuberculosis and mental patients are already covered under the insurance program when treated in general hospitals.
This is the point which I have just made in some detail and it is, surely, a reason for covering these illnesses, not for leaving them ineligible for assistance.
With regard to the general length of time spent by patients in both tuberculosis and mental hospitals, I should like to say that the period is rapidly decreasing. Statistics show that the average length of the stay in a general hospital is ten days. These are the statistics I previously used when giving figures of hospital beds available in 1962. A few years ago the average length of stay in a tuberculosis sanatorium was two years. I do not know the exact figure with regard to mental hospitals two or three years ago, but it was certainly longer than it is today. The reduction of time spent in hospital has been brought about in great measure by the discovery of new drugs. Then again, a great many patients are now being treated on an out-patient basis, rather than by being admitted to mental hospitals or tuberculosis sanatoria.
I should like to say a word about the royal commission on health services. This commission was appointed by the previous government and we are still awaiting its report. I certainly hope a report will be arriving soon, so that we may have not only a greater knowledge of this subject as a whole, but also some idea what the future treatment of tuberculosis and mental diseases is likely to be.
The last sentence in the hon. member's motion refers to the care and training of mentally retarded children. That is very good, and I certainly agree with the recommendation in this regard. I wonder whether the hon. member might not think it desirable to extend his proposal in this regard so as to include mentally retarded adults. In my own riding, though this does not present any great problem, it has presented some difficulties and recently a workshop was opened in the town of Burlington in connection with the care and attention of mentally retarded adults. These consist, generally speaking, of people in their late teens who require some supervision. It does not have to be psychiatric supervision, but it has to be supervision by understanding people to attempt to teach them a trade so that they can make a living, and function like ordinary citizens.

As I have mentioned, there is a great change in the circumstances surrounding treatment of both mental disease and tuberculosis. In the Canada Year Book, 1963-64, which I think most members received today, there are two paragraphs which are well worth putting on the record in this respect. Discussing psychiatric disorders and tuberculosis, the Year Book says:
Of the total of 76,486 psychiatric patients reported at Dec. 31, 1961, 35 per cent suffered from schizophrenia, the most frequent form of psychosis (insanity), 26 per cent suffered from other forms of psychosis and 29 per cent were mentally deficient. In most diagnostic classes, males outnumbered females; exceptions were certain psychoses, neuroses and drug addiction.
Of the 5,387 patients with respiratory tuberculosis on the books of tuberculosis institutions at the end of 1961, 63 per cent were males. Males outnumbered females in all age groups except for the ages from 0 to 19 years. The peak frequency for men (1,116) occurred in the 40-59 age group, and for women (688) in the 20-39 age group.
As I have said, there is a great change not only in the treatment of tubercular and mental patients but also in the type of patient whom the doctor is now meeting. With regard to both these diseases there is a change in the patient's outlook, in the number of admissions to hospitals, and so on. The number of admissions for tuberculosis treatment is gradually decreasing. This is probably because we now have good case finding methods, massive chest X-ray programs, the testing of school children and adequate follow-up care of patients. Because the length of stay in hospital has been greatly shortened we are now finding that beds in sanatoria are becoming empty. The reverse holds true in the case of provision for mental patients, more and more of whom are being admitted to hospital. I do not think this necessarily means that people are crazier now than they were a few years ago. I think it means that the general public is recognizing the fact that mental disease is a disease like any other. They are now coming forward in increasing numbers to request treatment either for themselves or for members of their families. They are asking for help so that doctors can treat them with the new drugs which are available.
Both tuberculosis and mental disease are being detected at an earlier date. This certainly leads to a greater expectation of success in the treatment of these diseases which, in turn, encourages the early reporting of cases. As I have mentioned, the time necessary to be spent in hospital in respect to both these diseases is much shorter than it was, and greatly improved treatment, both surgical and therapeutic, is available. If the people of Canada are to be encouraged to accept tuberculosis and, in particular, mental disease, as being, in essence, like any other disease, then, 20220-62
Expansion of Hospital Care Program surely, the government must be the first to take this attitude. The government must accept the fact that tuberculosis, mental disease and mental retardation are diseases like any others and should treat them like any other diseases under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the opportunity of being able to speak this afternoon in support of the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). To explain why I am so solidly in support may I go back into history for a few minutes. On November 2, 1933, Ernest Edward Winch was elected to the legislature of British Columbia for the constituency of Burnaby at the age of 55. He immediately made a study of provincial institutions and was the first member of the legislature to visit Essendale, that province's mental institution.
He was astounded at what he found. Men and women had been there for as long as 25 years who should have been discharged but were not because nobody was interested in them. He raised the issue in the legislature of British Columbia. I was the member for Vancouver East in the legislature at that time and I remember his saying: "Why do we not take people out of mental institutions as well as putting them in"? I can still remember the sneers and the jeers, and how he was almost howled down when he suggested in the British Columbia legislature that we should take people out of mental institutions as well as put them in.
Because the government of the day could not see the sense of his suggestion he went out and raised some money and bought a home. He furnished the home, hired a nurse and got the services of two doctors who believed in what he was doing. He then went to the mental institution, and because I was with him I remember well what happened. He said to the medical superintendent: "Have you any women here who should not be here"? The medical superintendent said: "Yes, how many do you want"? Over a period of three years women were signed out of the mental institution and taken into this home. After a three month period of rehabilitation they left and found jobs. Then others were taken from the mental institution.
November 2, 1933 was the beginning of the process which led to the establishment eventually in British Columbia of what is known as the Crease clinic. People no longer have to be committed directly to a mental institution. They can go voluntarily or by committal into a hospital for the mentally ill. The record is that in the majority of cases
966	HOUSE OF
Expansion of Hospital Care Program their mental illness is cured in three months just as a broken arm or leg or other physical disease can be cured.
Why have I introduced my remarks in this way? Because I did not understand and do not understand to this day why this and former federal governments have differentiated between mental illness and physical illness. One can break down mentally as well as physically, and in many instances he can be cured of a mental illness just as quickly as he can be cured of a physical illness.
Therefore I agree completely with the purpose of the motion which seeks to have the federal act changed in order that assistance may be given the provinces in caring for those who are mentally ill, just as the federal government now provides assistance in caring for those who are physically ill. The reclamation of the mentally ill, just as in the case of those who are physically ill, brings back into economic and social life exactly the same kind of people.
I also support strongly the latter part of the motion having to do with the care of mentally retarded children. Medical science has proved that many times a child who is mentally retarded can, with proper treatment, care and education, make a useful contribution to society and lead a better life as an individual. Yet what is the situation? So far as British Columbia is concerned, the situation is one of the most vicious, damnable and heinous of which I am aware. There are hundreds of mentally retarded children awaiting admission to the only institution we have in British Columbia. They cannot get admission, first, because there are not the facilities and, second, because there are not the trained personnel. Surely such care and treatment should not be the financial obligation of the provinces only, because a child or adult is a citizen not only of its own locality and province but of Canada. The assisting of one mentally retarded child will result in the addition of a most important asset to the country as a whole, irrespective of the benefit to the child itself.
I fail completely to understand why the responsibility for mentally retarded children should be wholly provincial. I say it is an out and out disgrace that the federal government should allow this situation to continue. In our province there are over 700 retarded children waiting for admission but who cannot get in, and not one cent is paid by the federal government on behalf of those children. From the knowledge I gained as a member of the B.C. legislature for 20 years, and having visited that institution every year, I know that these children can be helped to a great extent and need not have to stay there


all their lives; but if they are not attended to then they will have to spend the rest of their lives either there or in a mental institution.
Whether you look at the matter from a moral, social or financial viewpoint, surely the federal government has a responsibility toward the mentally ill and retarded children, just the same as it has toward those who are physically ill and for whom the government makes a contribution under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. From any angle you look at the matter, Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any basis whatsoever on which the House of Commons or the federal government can refuse to accept responsibility for the three categories of people referred to in the motion now before us. I sincerely hope the motion will not be talked out.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks with regard to what has been said by the mover of the motion and other speakers so far in the debate. We have, of course, the greatest sympathy with the objective that has been put forward of relieving suffering, and especially to do something to improve the facilities for the treatment of mental illness in Canada.
We also have to bear other considerations in mind. Many, many things can be done in the field of human welfare. Within a recent period this parliament passed a measure which has added a fairly substantial amount to the old age pension. We all were pleased to support it. We have to think in terms of the budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will present to this house this evening. We are talking, in terms of this resolution-I have not done any precise cost calculation-of something of the order of $100 million per year, if we implement the resolution as it is framed. We are all in favour of doing everything that is possible, consistent with the growth of Canada and the prosperity of this country and with the achievement of a relative measure of stability in our public accounts which we certainly recognize as desirable at this stage of Canada's development.
I am particularly concerned with one aspect of this resolution which I think members of this house should consider in greater detail. The resolution refers to sufficient funds to provide for the adequate treatment of the mentally ill, those people suffering from tuberculosis and the care and training of mentally retarded children. I should like to speak for a moment about the care of those patients suffering from tuberculosis. From the information available to us, it is quite clear that

this disease is declining in incidence in Canada. I have a statistical report of the bureau of statistics for 1961 in my hand. This report indicates that between 1960 and 1961, for example, three institutions in the province of Quebec were converted from tuberculosis care to other types of care, two to chronic institutions and the third for the treatment of mental illness. In this period there was a 13 per cent decline in days of care in tuberculosis institutions, which is very revealing and encouraging to us.
From all reports, this is one disease that does not suffer from a lack of facilities in Canada. It is quite clear that the tremendous achievements of those who served in this field have resulted in this decline, and it is also a recognition of the standards of Canadian medicine and the standards of care in the institutions, as well as of the diligence of those who supported voluntary organizations who have gone out case-finding and so on. It is, as well, a general reflection of the standard of living in Canada, improved housing, improved nutrition and so on.
But we ask ourselves at this point, what is to be achieved by the inclusion of tuberculosis institutions under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act? I note from the same bureau of statistics publication that in the year 1961 15.6 per cent of the revenues of the institutions providing care came from federal government sources; 68.2 per cent of the revenues came from provincial government sources; 4 per cent from municipal governments. Looking on down the list, I find that less than 1 per cent, about eight tenths of 1 per cent, of the revenues of these institutions came from paying patients. Now, what would be the effect, I ask hon. members of this house, of the inclusion of a program in which there is, from all evidence, a satisfactory number of beds, satisfactory facilities for treatment and where there is a decline in the incidence of the disease? It still remains an important disease which cannot be neglected. If we were to sharply reduce the service facilities it would be a serious mistake, we all agree.
The fact is, however, there is nothing like the case to be made for the extension of services to tuberculosis that there is for its extension in respect of mental illness or mental retardation. I submit that the effect of including this program would be a fiscal measure. It would give fiscal relief to the provinces. It would not extend the services. It would not relieve charges on the patients. It would have the pure and simple result of a new alignment of fiscal responsibilities. This may well be one of the matters that the Minister of Finance may wish to raise with 20220-62J
Expansion of Hospital Care Program the provincial ministers at the federal-provincial conference, because of the demand for greater sources of revenue and the demand for higher grants from the federal government. This is surely a fiscal matter. Surely, the effect of including tuberculosis institutions, as proposed in this resolution, would be a fiscal matter. It would not have any significant effect upon the care of persons suffering from this disease.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the situation with regard to mental illness is different in many respects. It is not different, however, in regard to the general incidence, shall we say, or proportion of revenues received from different sources. The revenue sources are similar to those of tuberculosis institutions. The dominion bureau of statistics report for 1961 shows that 94.6 per cent of the revenues of these institutions came from public sources; 5 per cent from the federal government; 88.2 per cent from the provincial governments; 1.4 per cent from municipal governments, and patient payments amounted in this case to 3.3 per cent. This source is significant in the case of mental illness, but it still does not amount to a serious proportion in terms of the cost of operating mental institutions.
The case for the extension of federal aid in regard to mental illness is a case which has to be related to the extension and improvement of the quality of the services. None of us in this house who have looked at mental institutions can deny that there is a great job to be done here. However, the thing which we have to remember is the philosophy of government. It is not the intention of the federal government to own and1 operate hospitals. It is the intention, I am sure, to make sure that the health services' which have been traditionally and primarily" a provincial responsibility under our constitutional development are provided at the level which is most capable of providing them and supervising them.
Now, mental illness is provided for in four basic types of institution. There is the general mental hospital, the more modern concept of psychiatric hospital, training schools for retarded children and psychiatric wings in general hospitals. When the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was passed by this parliament, the framers of the act looked very carefully at the situation in regard to mental illness. They were not lacking in sympathy by any means. They were, however, to some degree, guided by the practical considerations of the treasury, and this must always be a factor in government. They were concerned also about the healthy and orderly development of a pattern of service to give the best possible care for mental

Expansion of Hospital Care Program illness. The psychiatric units in general hospitals are part of the benefits of hospital insurance. These units, which traditionally are for short term mental illness-the average days' stay the last time I looked at the statistics was about 23 days, which is more than twice that for general hospital admission- have been expanding. These facilities are closely integrated with the community. They are extremely well adapted to provide a good pattern of service. The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act has stimulated a very healthy and necessary expansion of this type of facility.
In so far as training schools for the mentally retarded are concerned, there is a dividing line between the educational responsibility of the province and the health responsibility. In the health field, there has been a recognition more and more of the very positive role of the senior government in providing financial assistance or grants in aid. The previous speaker on the government side, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), detailed the form of national health grants and the benefits under the act which are available.
I cannot help repeating that those of us who have had any experience at the local level with the tremendous gap in educational facilities for the mentally retarded, recognize that here is an area where a great deal needs to be done. A child with a certain i.q. can go into the school system and receive grants. The child just below that level too frequently and sadly is denied even the minimum educational opportunities, with the great tragedy that follows from that.
There is a need for initiative to be taken by the provinces in extending grants for mentally retarded children, but a pattern of federal aid cannot be purely and simply fiscal relief for the provinces. We would be negligent in our responsibilities to the taxpayers if we were to adopt a resolution which merely has the effect of channelling more federal money out, without making sure that the necessary co-ordinating of services follows.
It is a limited initiative which this house can take in the field of education, and there is a very great need to call attention to provincial responsibilities in this regard. My concern in dealing with this measure is simply that we must not fall into the trap of adopting something which could have the result of merely providing fiscal relief. The emphasis on federal funds must be to encourage and assist in filling the gaps that now exist, in extending into areas where services are now inadequate, and in helping the provinces to do those things which the


hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) so eloquently described as being necessary.
We are not lacking in human sympathy when we call attention to the need for orderly development. We are not lacking in human sympathy when we say we must not vote money without making sure of a balanced program.

So far as the procedures are concerned whereby we can achieve these ends, it is my humble estimation and belief that a private member's bill is not the ultimate solution in this respect. As the hon. member knows, the report of the royal commission on health services, which should embrace the entire field, will shortly come

before us, and we hope it will result in a solution for this deplorable problem.
On all sides of the house and in all parties we are generally committed to the axioms of the welfare state. Great programs of welfare and social benefits are accepted by all parties, yet in those limited areas where the vast body of people are not represented, such areas as mental health, alcoholism and dope addiction, we know we will not gain a great number of votes by bringing in remedial measures. Alcoholism, dope addiction, and mental retardation do not strike the vast majority of people, but I suggest that if we are sincere adherents of social welfare and better standards of well-being we should begin with those who are the least able to look after themselves.
As politicians, it may be those are the very last people with whom we are concerned, because they are not politically popular, they do not control any large block of votes and, as I say, the vast majority of the population is not going to give us political approbation for helping such people.
I suggest that in this area of mental retardation, and specifically with respect to children, we cannot take very great pride federally or provincially in what we have done in this supposedly enlightened and advanced country. It is my hope that when the report of the royal commission comes in and is debated in this house, the hon. member who proposed this bill, and others who have supported his ideas, will give their approval to the kind of remedy which will do something for the problems of children who are mentally retarded.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved:

speechtext:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other hon. members spoke about Jack Garland, and how much he will be missed by all hon. members of this house. I shall not repeat
The Budget-Mr. Gordon what has been said, but I could not begin my budget speech without adding a few words about the feeling of loss and sadness that I share with all hon. members in not having Jack with us tonight. Inevitably there is a very close relationship between ministers of finance and ministers of national revenue. In my case I shall always be grateful to Jack Garland for his advice, his common sense, his sound judgment, his friendship and his cheerfulness, and support when times were tough. Jack Garland sat in on the many meetings preceding the preparation of the budget that I am about to deliver. He made a great contribution to it, as he did to everything he was involved in or associated with. He was a sensible, quiet man who was universally respected. Jack Garland was everybody's friend.
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members can take sastisfaction from the improvement that has been occurring in economic conditions in Canada and from the optimism with which we can view the immediate future. Unemployment is still too high, and in the Atlantic provinces and eastern Quebec it is much too high. But it is lower almost everywhere than it has been for some years. The deficit in our current account balance of payments with other countries is still too large but it is smaller than it has been since 1954. The prospects for the current year are good; indeed, in most parts of Canada they are very good. Employment, production and incomes should all be substantially higher than last year for the country as a whole.
Many changes in fiscal and economic policies were called for in the circumstances this parliament faced last spring. It was necessary to move quickly on a number of fronts, and understandably some of the proposals that were put forward were questioned at the time.

These measures have contributed to the increase in economic activity that has occurred and to the reduction of unemployment. They should be continued and they will be.
The winter house building bonus was so effective that a limit had to be put on the

The Budget-Mr. Gordon number of houses to be financed in order to avoid congestion in markets this spring. The accelerated rates of capital cost allowances have been a powerful inducement to increased expenditures on industrial building and equipment. Already the measures introduced to stimulate the automobile industry have borne fruit. The new policy will mean greater investment, more production and more jobs in Canada in the future. The extended program of assistance in building vocational schools is proceeding at a rapid pace.

speechtext:
I am delighted we have unanimity on some of these matters.
Other policies which we said would require some time before becoming fully effective are beginning to take hold. I refer to the efforts to encourage our secondary manufacturing industries through the new Department of Industry; to the incentives designed to stimulate activity in areas of slower growth; and to the work that will be done, and the new jobs that will be created, as a result of funds made available by the municipal development and loan board and the Atlantic development board. All these policies, as I say, have proved their worth. We must now consolidate our gains and plan for steady growth.
Before reviewing the state of the economy and the prospects for the future, I should like to recall several of the government's major objectives in economic policy, which I am sure are generally supported by the members of this house.
Our first goal is high level unemployment-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It must be a bad translation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I feel, Mr. Speaker, in the same class as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when he sometimes refers to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). As I was trying to say, our first goal is high level employment, the highest we can expect to reach and maintain; employment in good jobs where we can produce efficiently. This requires not only jobs but men and women qualified to fill them.
Our second, and related goal, is a high level of economic growth, the highest we can expect to sustain over a long period. This will help employment and will bring better living standards, but it will require foresight and skill in economic management both private and public.
Third, we want to gain all the advantages that go with expanded international trade, both exports and imports. In the process we want to see our transactions with other countries on current account brought into better

balance. Continued deficits in our balance of payments on current account make it more difficult to attain high level employment and render us vulnerable to changes in the supply of capital available to us.
Fourth, we want to maintain general stability in our price levels and the value of our currency, for that is necessary to steady progress and to the protection of the savings of the people.
Our budget policies and measures, as well as others affecting our economic affairs, should be fashioned and considered with these objectives in mind. We should add to them another that is partially economic, partially political in the broadest sense of that word. We Canadians realize we cannot live in isolation; we are part of an interdependent world; we are members of the greatest peacetime alliance in history; we live in one of the most open and unrestricted economies in the world; we earn much of our living in foreign trade; and we benefit from foreign investment to a degree probably greater than any other nation. We recognize the advantages and obligations of these relationships with others. But we believe that we can and should combine them with a full participation by Canadians in the management and direction of all aspects of our own affairs.

We can look back on the economic developments of 1963 and early 1964 with considerable satisfaction. Many new records have been achieved-in employment and trade, in agriculture and industry. More men and women have jobs; their take-home pay is higher; fewer fail to find the jobs they are looking for; and the number of young people in training to acquire up to date skills is steadily expanding.
Last year we built our budget estimates of government revenues on the assumption that total Canadian production and expenditure- our gross national product-would be about 5 per cent higher in 1963 than in the previous year, assuming a normal crop and reasonably stable prices. I am glad to say that our assumption about prices proved correct. Canadian crops far exceeded anyone's expectations. Economic activity in other sectors was more buoyant than we had anticipated. Accordingly, the increase in total output in 1963 turned out to be, not 5 per cent, but about 6 per cent.
Not only did we have a record wheat crop last year, more than 720 million bushels-
Call that a record?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far-but it was coupled with record overseas sales. Vast quantities of grain are being moved to ocean ports. In the

field of prices and costs the degree of stability that we have been achieving is greater than that of any of our overseas competitors and is about the same as that of the United States.
Same as last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Details are to be found in the white paper on pages 38-40. It is worth noting that, for the latest month for which comparable figures are available-December-our consumer price index showed exactly the same movement in comparison with the previous year-1.7 per cent-as the American index. The latest 12 month increase for Britain is 1.9 per cent, for France 5.7 per cent and for Japan 4.9 per cent.
Thanks to the degree of stability we have maintained, much of Canadian industry is now competitive with that of other countries. Clearly we must strive to keep our costs down and to increase our productivity.
Our favourable competitive position is reflected in the fact that our merchandise exports in 1963 rose 11 per cent over the previous year, while imports rose only 6 per cent. In the result we had a favourable balance of $484 million on merchandise account-the largest since 1952. The sharp increase in our exports of manufactured products was particularly encouraging.
On travel account, we had run deficits for more than a decade, but in 1963 we earned a surplus of $13 million. On the other hand, we had an adverse balance in respect of interest and dividends amounting to $614 million, continuing the upward trend of the post-war years.
As a result of these and other changes our current account deficits with other countries, which stood at $848 million in 1962, was reduced by more than one third, down to a level of $521 million, in 1963.
Personal incomes rose steadily last year; private spending and saving both increased. Canadians chose to buy more Canadian goods; a number of Canadian industries improved their share of the Canadian market, taking advantage of the improvement in their competitive position. Canadians also decided to save more-a slightly higher proportion of their incomes than previously-and they were thus in a position to play a rather larger part in financing Canadian expansion.
Industrial and manufacturing production both increased by some 5.6 per cent in 1963 over 1962. Expansion of private investment in plant and equipment was also well maintained.
The general price stability to which I have referred was matched by general financial stability. In other periods of general economic expansion we have experienced some hardening of interest rates, a natural result of
The Budget-Mr. Gordon increased competition amongst borrowers for available funds. This did not happen last year. Interest rates at the end of 1963 and in the early part of this year were at about the same levels as a year before, some slightly higher and others slightly lower. The spread between Canadian and United States interest rates narrowed appreciably particularly on short term issues. Growth of the money supply, which had been reversed by the financial crisis of June 1962, was resumed; during 1963 the total money supply expanded by 9 per cent; over the two year period, 1962 and 1963, the total increase was somewhat less than the 14 per cent increase in the gross national product.
While economic activity, and with it the number of available jobs, increased in 1963, so did the number of people seeking work. However, the increase in jobs outran the increase in job-seekers. From an average level of 5.9 per cent, almost 6 per cent, the previous year, and 7.2 per cent in 1961, average unemployment in 1963 fell to 5.5 per cent.
Moreover, the reduction of the average of unemployment for the year does not tell the whole story. While economic activity was strong throughout 1963 it was strongest in the final months. As the house is aware, we have recently broken through the 5 per cent unemployment barrier on a seasonally adjusted basis for the first time since 1957. As we enter 1964, the economic momentum is even stronger than it was throughout 1963.
This does not mean we can afford to be complacent. Our international deficit has been cut down, but it still remained more than half a billion dollars in 1963. And a level of unemployment around 5 per cent represents only progress by comparison with previous performance. We must do better in the months and years ahead.
If we are to do better we must recognize that the nature of our unemployment problem is changing. Over-all national averages mask important differences that exist between the various regions of Canada. At the beginning of this year the seasonally adjusted figure for unemployment in Canada was just below 5 per cent. However, according to our best current estimates, the figure for British Columbia, again on a seasonally adjusted basis, was just above 4 per cent. For the prairies it was around 2 per cent. In Ontario it had fallen to about 3 per cent, but in Quebec, where the increase in the labour force had been quite exceptional, it was probably about 6 per cent. For the Atlantic region, the figure while falling, was probably still as high as 8 per cent.
The wide diversity of these figures and the prospect for the current year suggests that

The Budget-Mr. Gordon broad, general attacks on unemployment will be less useful now than they have been in the past. Accordingly our plans and policies are increasingly designed to meet the special needs of areas of the country or groups of the population confronted with special difficulties and problems.
The figures for the 1964 capital investment outlook published last week, show that a substantial increase over last year is intended by businessmen, home owners, and governments; forebodings lest, as a result of tax changes announced last year, investment would wither away have, of course, not materialized. It is reassuring to note that the greatest increase in investment is expected to take place in the province where, in absolute terms, the number of unemployed is at the moment greatest, that is in the province of Quebec.
In regard to the balance of payments too we must recognize the nature of the problem confronting us. Our extraordinary sales of grain to Russia and other countries have greatly helped to improve our current account position, while some of our policies designed to encourage a more permanent improvement are beginning to take effect. However, we cannot assume that sales of grain will continue indefinitely at current levels. Therefore we must maintain our efforts to strengthen our balance of payments by measures of a longer term nature.
On the capital side of our balance of payments we have now seen in two successive years how vulnerable we are to sudden changes in the inflow of funds. In July last the announcement of the proposed United States interest equalization tax caused a very sharp crisis in our exchange and capital markets because our vital dependence on a large inflow of capital to pay our bills in the United States was widely recognized. The situation was eased by the proposal to exempt new Canadian issues. However uncertainties relating to this tax while it remains before congress have held back Canadian borrowing in the United States. It is still difficult to tell what the final effect of the tax will be on the movements of capital between the United States and Canada.
Despite these cautionary remarks a careful review of the economic outlook at home and abroad gives us cause for optimism. We see good reason to expect that in 1964 the general growth of the economy will be maintained and the good progress of the year just past will be repeated.
At the same time we obviously cannot anticipate another record harvest such as we had last year. In forecasting our revenues and expenditures we have worked on the assumption that we will have a normal harvest and an increase in gross national product, apart

from farm production of about 6J per cent. Taking farm and non-farm production both into account we assume an over-all growth of 5i per cent.

Before turning from economic affairs to fiscal matters, I should direct the attention of the house briefly to trade and tariff policy.
The United Nations conference on trade and development which opens in Geneva next week will focus on the special trade and development problems of the economically less developed nations of the world. One of the greatest problems of our age is to find practical ways of raising the standards of living of these nations. I should like to assure honourable members that Canada will play an active part in this United Nations conference. It will be our purpose to find effective methods for improving the trade opportunities of the less developed countries, without disruption of established industries in the more advanced countries. Clearly this will not be easy. For some years Canada has been accepting a substantial measure of imports from low-cost countries. We shall urge other advanced countries to do likewise.
As the house will be aware, the Kennedy round of trade negotiations is expected to get under way in the next few months. The prospects are that it will rank with the important trade negotiations that have taken place under the auspices of the GATT since the end of the war. While it has been agreed to conduct these negotiations on the basis of across-the-board tariff reductions by the United States and the European trade groups, agreement has not yet been reached on such matters as the depth of the basic tariff cut, the problem of trade in agricultural products, and the problem of tariff disparities between these countries. Accordingly, the full scope and nature of these negotiations remain to be settled.
Canada will not of course be negotiating on the basis of across-the-board linear tariff cuts. Our trading partners have recognized that such a system would not be appropriate for countries such as Canada. For us the objective is an exchange of concessions of equivalent value. Our participation should, I suggest, be guided by the following considerations.
First is the principle of reciprocity. There must be a reasonable balance between concessions obtained and those which we grant, which must be judged in terms of their practical effects or trade. Moreover, account must be taken of the degree of adjustment and time required to adapt to tariff reductions in terms of shifts in resources and employment.

A second key consideration is that the outcome of these negotiations should contribute to the balanced growth of the Canadian economy. Certainly we shall be seeking to expand the opportunities for our traditional exports of raw materials and foodstuffs. But these negotiations will be more concerned with manufactured products and we must keep clearly in mind that the expansion of efficient secondary industries is necessary to provide adequate employment opportunities for Canada's growing labour force. For this reason we shall be looking for those particular tariff reductions abroad which will open up new export markets for the products of our secondary industries. This will help them to achieve better economies of scale, which are vital to the attainment of cost efficiency.
A third important consideration is that there must be a reasonable balance between concessions given and concessions gained for the various sectors and regions of the Canadian economy. Each of the major productive sectors should get some benefit from and should make its contribution to the negotiations. This should be broadly true also for the various regions.
A fourth consideration relates to our balance of payments position. A successful tariff negotiation should help all the participating countries to become more efficient and more productive. But clearly, it cannot help them all to improve their balance of payments position. In our situation of continuing large current account deficits, we must be especially careful that any tariff bargain we strike does not aggravate our balance of payments position.
Guided by these considerations, Canada will play an important part in the Kennedy round. As hon. members are aware, a trade negotiating committee of experienced officers has been set up to assist the government in the conduct of these negotiations. Under its direction arrangements have been made to hear the views of Canadian industries and other interested parties, so that our preparations will take into account the most complete and up to date advice and information.

In addition to taking into account the economic and financial situation, the government must have regard to the position and requirements of provincial governments when making plans both for expenditure and taxation. Earlier in the history of our nation it may have been possible for the federal and provincial governments to proceed about their own affairs without concern for the other, except for occasional arguments over the constitutional subsidies. But now the public
The Budget-Mr. Gordon expects so much from both levels of government that they often appear to be in competition with one another. To overcome this each must now take into account the demands upon the other. At times in the past the provinces have recognized that we had special and urgent requirements for war and defence and for major social security programs. More recently the federal government has recognized that the provinces have urgent requirements in the fields of education, health and highways, and has acted accordingly. Both sides must recognize that Canadians cannot afford to do everything at once. In a federal system such as ours there must be an effort made to work out priorities by co-operation.
This recognition on our part of the requirements of the provinces must not be mistaken for an abnegation of federal responsibilities. Canada needs to have both strong provincial governments and a strong federal government. As I say, the government of Canada must remain strong and dynamic, both in its effective jurisdiction and in finance. This was intended in the constitution; it is even more necessary today.
Parliament will be asked to make the necessary changes in our laws to implement the new equalization formula for 1964-65, which was put before the conference with the provinces in November, and to carry out the undertaking given by the government in regard to the larger share of death duties to be assigned to the provinces.
In our spring meeting of the conference to begin on March 31 we shall be considering among other things shared-cost programs and their relation to our fiscal arrangements. Our general position was put by the Prime Minister in his published statement in November. It remains to examine how it may be implemented in particular cases. If the provinces so wish, we are prepared to transfer to them full financial responsibility for some of these established shared-cost programs of a continuing nature, and to make suitable fiscal adjustments either in a larger share of the direct tax fields or by changes in, or supplements to, the equalization payments.
These financial adjustments must be fair both to the provincial and the federal treasuries. We appreciate the importance and value of joint programs. We have no desire, however, to go on indefinitely levying taxes simply to pay for programs that are well established and well within provincial jurisdiction. It is better that, within the limits of their own fiscal capacities, the provinces should levy the taxes required for such programs, assisted where necessary by equalization payments.
The Budget-Mr. Gordon

I come now to a consideration of our revenues and expenditures for the fiscal year now concluding. A detailed report is given in the budget papers that were tabled last Thursday. At this time of year the figures are, of course, preliminary and subject to change. Tonight I propose to refer only to the more important items.
In the budget speech last June, expenditures were forecast at $6,845 million. The revenue estimates, as revised on July 8, were $6,190 million. On this basis, a deficit was anticipated of $655 million, together with a deficit of $25 million for the old age security fund.
It now appears that our budgetary revenue will be $6,207 million. On the other hand, when we include the charging to expenditures of $76 million pension liabilities created by pay increases for the armed forces, and $48 million inventory losses on farm products held in storage, which I explained in the house on March 6, our budgetary expenditures now appear likely to be about $6,892 million. Consequently, the deficit for the year is expected to be about $685 million. It would have been appreciably less than the forecast but for the large "write-offs" I have mentioned.
The forecasts for the old age security fund were affected, of course, by the decision to increase old age pensions by $10 per month, effective October 1, and by the increase in the old age security tax on personal incomes from 3 to 4 per cent, effective January 1, 1964. As a result of these changes, revenues credited to the fund were $15 million higher, pension payments were $54 million higher, and the deficit was $64 million. This will be made up in the next few years; in the meantime it has been met by a temporary loan to the fund.
It sounds like us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It sounds like you?
What you said about us last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not quite hear the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings reminiscing.
In addition to the revenues and expenditures that are included in what are known as budgetary accounts, the government disburses large sums for loans, investments and advances for a variety of purposes, and receives substantial sums from various sources

that do not constitute revenues, since at the same time they create liabilities or represent repayment of debts due the crown. During 1963-64, these cash disbursements included $122 million advanced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and $72 million loaned to the Farm Credit Corporation, as well as many other items set forth in detail in the white paper. To meet these outlays, large sums were available from the repayment of loans, including $111 million from the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, and from various annuity, insurance and pension accounts. In all, our nonbudgetary receipts exceeded non-budgetary disbursements by $166 million.
In explaining our total cash requirements I should take this opportunity to note that for the most part our budgetary revenues and expenditures involve cash receipts and disbursements. While our expenditures do include some charges of a bookkeeping nature, these are offset by equal credits to nonbudgetary accounts. When all are taken together, excluding the sale or redemption of debt securities, we obtain our total cash requirements. For 1963-64 the budgetary deficit of $685 million, offset by the net nonbudgetary receipts of $166 million, resulted in an over-all cash requirement of $519 million. It is expected that this net disbursement of cash during the year will have been somewhat less than the increase of $737 million in our outstanding debt, with the result that our cash balances will be some $218 million higher at the end of the year than they were at the beginning.
I turn now to consider the budget outlook for the next fiscal year. With the economic outlook as I have described it, and with no change in our present tax laws, I would forecast our budget revenues at $6,705 million, almost $500 million more than for the current fiscal year. With the consent of the house, I should like at this point to insert the usual table in Hansard showing our estimated revenues before tax changes and comparing them with revenues in 1963-64.
I should point out further that, since there will be other occasions tonight, Mr. Speaker, when I propose to present tabular material, perhaps the house might be prepared to give its consent now to having these tables printed as appendices in Hansard.

Agreed.
